name: API Style Guide Quality Rubric
description: LLM-as-a-Judge rubric for evaluating the quality, completeness, and usability of API style guides. Based on industry best practices from Stoplight, Zalando, Microsoft, Google, and PayPal.

categories.name: Content Coverage
categories.description: Evaluates whether the style guide covers the six essential domains that every API style guide should address.
categories.evaluationPrompt: Evaluate whether this API style guide covers the essential content domains. Check for presence and depth of coverage in each area.
passCriteria: Covers architectural style (REST, GraphQL, gRPC, etc.)
Specifies API description format requirements (OpenAPI, AsyncAPI, etc.)
Defines naming conventions for resources, fields, and parameters
Standardizes error handling (status codes, error format, messages)
Addresses authentication and authorization patterns
Clarifies versioning strategy (URI, header, semantic versioning)
partialCriteria: Covers 4-5 of the 6 essential domains
Some domains are mentioned but lack depth
Missing coverage for security or versioning
failCriteria: Major gaps in naming or error handling
No mention of API description format

pass.excerpt: The guide includes dedicated sections for: REST principles (Chapter 1), OpenAPI specification requirements (Chapter 2), Naming conventions with snake_case for fields and kebab-case for URLs (Chapter 3), RFC 7807 Problem+JSON error format (Chapter 4), OAuth 2.0 and API key authentication (Chapter 5), and URL-based versioning with deprecation policy (Chapter 6).
pass.reasoning: All six essential domains are covered with dedicated sections providing detailed guidance.

partial.excerpt: The guide covers REST principles, naming conventions, and error handling, but authentication is only briefly mentioned and versioning strategy is not defined.
partial.reasoning: Good coverage of core topics but missing depth in security and versioning domains.

fail.excerpt: The guide only discusses naming conventions and provides some examples of endpoints. No mention of error handling, authentication, or versioning.
fail.reasoning: Covers only 1-2 domains, missing critical guidance for production APIs.

categories.name: Structure & Navigation
categories.description: Evaluates the organizational quality and navigability of the style guide.
categories.evaluationPrompt: Evaluate the structure and navigability of this API style guide. Consider whether users can quickly find relevant guidance.
passCriteria: Has clear table of contents or navigation structure
Uses consistent heading hierarchy
Groups related rules into logical sections/categories
Provides cross-references between related rules
Includes search or index capability (for digital guides)
partialCriteria: Has table of contents but inconsistent section organization
Some cross-references but not comprehensive
Logical grouping exists but could be improved
failCriteria: No table of contents or navigation aids
Rules are presented as a flat, unorganized list

pass.excerpt: The guide features a comprehensive table of contents, numbered rules (e.g., RULE-001), categories (Naming, HTTP Methods, Errors, etc.), and hyperlinks between related rules. Each section starts with an overview and lists its rules.
pass.reasoning: Excellent navigability with multiple ways to find and navigate to relevant content.

partial.excerpt: The guide has sections but no table of contents. Rules are grouped but lack consistent numbering or identifiers.
partial.reasoning: Basic organization exists but navigation could be significantly improved.

fail.excerpt: All rules are listed sequentially in a single document with no headings, categories, or identifiers.
fail.reasoning: No structural organization makes finding specific guidance very difficult.

categories.name: Rule Quality & Clarity
categories.description: Evaluates whether individual rules are clear, actionable, and well-explained.
categories.evaluationPrompt: Evaluate the quality of individual rules in this API style guide. Consider clarity, actionability, and completeness.
passCriteria: Each rule has a clear, concise title
Rules provide rationale explaining WHY the rule exists
Rules are actionable with specific guidance on HOW to comply
Uses RFC 2119 keywords (MUST, SHOULD, MAY) consistently
Rules include severity/priority levels
Each rule has a unique identifier for reference
partialCriteria: Rules are clear but lack rationale
Inconsistent use of RFC 2119 keywords
Some rules are vague or lack specific guidance
Missing rule identifiers or severity levels
failCriteria: Rules are not actionable (what vs. how)

pass.excerpt: RULE-118: Use snake_case for JSON property names. Severity: Error. Rationale: Consistent naming improves API usability and enables automated tooling. Property names MUST use lowercase letters and underscores only. Example: customer_id, billing_address.
pass.reasoning: Rule has ID, title, severity, rationale, RFC 2119 keyword, and example.

partial.excerpt: Use snake_case for properties. This helps with consistency.
partial.reasoning: Guidance is clear but lacks ID, severity, detailed rationale, and examples.

fail.reasoning: Vague guidance without specific format, rationale, or actionable instruction.

categories.name: Examples & Code Samples
categories.description: Evaluates whether the guide provides sufficient good and bad examples to illustrate rules.
categories.evaluationPrompt: Evaluate the quality and coverage of examples in this API style guide.
passCriteria: Provides both good (correct) and bad (incorrect) examples
Examples are realistic and representative of actual API usage
Code samples are properly formatted and syntax-highlighted
Examples cover common use cases and edge cases
Examples show before/after for migration guidance
partialCriteria: Has examples but only shows correct patterns (no anti-patterns)
Examples are too simplistic or toy examples
Inconsistent formatting of code samples
Limited coverage of edge cases

pass.reasoning: Clear good/bad contrast with explanation of what makes the bad example incorrect.

partial.reasoning: Only shows correct pattern without contrasting incorrect patterns.

fail.excerpt: The guide states to use snake_case but all examples show camelCase.
fail.reasoning: Examples contradict the stated rules, creating confusion.

categories.name: Enforceability & Tooling
categories.description: Evaluates whether rules can be automatically enforced or checked.
categories.evaluationPrompt: Evaluate whether the rules in this style guide are enforceable through automated tooling.
passCriteria: Rules indicate whether they are lintable or require manual review
Provides Spectral/OpenAPI ruleset or equivalent
References specific tool configurations for enforcement
Distinguishes between deterministic checks and judgment calls
Includes CI/CD integration guidance
partialCriteria: Some rules are clearly lintable but no tooling provided
Mentions tooling but doesn't provide configuration
Inconsistent classification of rule enforceability
failCriteria: Rules are entirely subjective with no linting possibility

pass.excerpt: This rule is enforced by Spectral rule 'operation-operationId'. Add to your .spectral.yaml: extends: ['@zalando/zally-rules']
pass.reasoning: Clear indication of enforcement mechanism with specific tool configuration.

partial.excerpt: This rule can be checked with a linter. [No specific tool mentioned]
partial.reasoning: Acknowledges linting possibility but doesn't provide actionable configuration.

fail.excerpt: All rules require human review during code review.
fail.reasoning: No automated enforcement, entirely manual compliance.

categories.name: Guide Versioning & Evolution
categories.description: Evaluates whether the style guide itself is versioned and designed for evolution.
categories.evaluationPrompt: Evaluate whether this style guide is versioned and designed to evolve over time.
passCriteria: Guide has explicit version number
Includes changelog or history of changes
Has deprecation policy for rules
Provides migration guidance for rule changes
Single source of truth (no multiple outdated versions)
partialCriteria: Has version number but no changelog
Deprecation mentioned but not systematically applied
Some historical context but incomplete
failCriteria: No process for updating or deprecating rules

pass.excerpt: Version 2.0.0 (2024-01-15). See CHANGELOG.md for history. Rule Z-123 deprecated in v1.8, replaced by Z-456. Migration: Change from PUT to PATCH for partial updates.
pass.reasoning: Clear version, changelog reference, deprecation info, and migration guidance.

partial.reasoning: Has version but no changelog or deprecation process.

fail.excerpt: API Guidelines (no version). Note: This is one of three guideline documents.
fail.reasoning: No version and multiple documents suggest inconsistency.

categories.name: Completeness & Depth
categories.description: Evaluates whether the guide provides sufficient depth for complex topics.
categories.evaluationPrompt: Evaluate the depth and completeness of guidance provided for complex API design topics.
passCriteria: Addresses common edge cases and exceptions
Provides decision trees or flowcharts for complex decisions
Includes guidance for API evolution and breaking changes
Covers both happy path and error scenarios
Addresses internationalization and localization
partialCriteria: Covers main scenarios but limited edge case guidance
Some complex topics are oversimplified
Evolution guidance exists but incomplete
failCriteria: Complex topics are ignored or deferred
No guidance for API evolution or breaking changes

pass.excerpt: For pagination, use cursor-based pagination for large datasets (see decision tree). For collections < 1000 items, offset pagination is acceptable. For breaking changes, follow the deprecation timeline: announce 6 months before, add Sunset header, maintain deprecated endpoint for 12 months.
pass.reasoning: Provides nuanced guidance with decision criteria and detailed process for complex scenarios.

partial.excerpt: Use pagination for large collections. Avoid breaking changes when possible.
partial.reasoning: Mentions topics but lacks specific guidance or decision criteria.

fail.excerpt: All GET requests should return data.
fail.reasoning: Trivial guidance that doesn't address real API design challenges.

categories.name: Internal Consistency
categories.description: Evaluates whether the guide is internally consistent and free of contradictions.
categories.evaluationPrompt: Check for internal consistency within the API style guide. Look for contradictions, conflicting advice, or inconsistent terminology.
passCriteria: No contradictory rules
Consistent terminology throughout
Consistent use of RFC 2119 keywords
Examples align with stated rules
Cross-references are accurate
partialCriteria: Minor inconsistencies in terminology
Some examples don't perfectly match rules
Mostly consistent but with a few conflicts
failCriteria: Inconsistent use of terms (e.g., endpoint vs. resource vs. URI)
Conflicting severity levels for similar rules

pass.excerpt: The guide consistently uses 'resource' for REST nouns, 'endpoint' for URL paths, and 'operation' for HTTP method + path combinations. All examples follow stated naming conventions.
pass.reasoning: Consistent terminology and alignment between rules and examples.

partial.excerpt: Most examples use snake_case as required, but the error handling section uses camelCase in its examples.
partial.reasoning: Mostly consistent but with isolated inconsistencies.

fail.excerpt: Rule 5 says 'always use plural nouns for collections' but Rule 23 says 'singleton resources use singular nouns for collections when semantically appropriate'.
fail.reasoning: Contradictory rules create confusion about correct approach.

categories.name: Accessibility & Tone
categories.description: Evaluates whether the guide is accessible to its intended audience and uses appropriate tone.
categories.evaluationPrompt: Evaluate the accessibility and tone of this API style guide. Consider whether it is appropriate for its audience.
passCriteria: Written at appropriate technical level for audience
Tone matches organizational culture (formal/informal as appropriate)
Avoids unnecessary jargon without sacrificing precision
Includes glossary for technical terms
Available in accessible formats
partialCriteria: Generally accessible but some sections too technical
Tone is inconsistent across sections
Missing glossary for some terms

pass.excerpt: Use PATCH for partial updates. (See Glossary: PATCH). This allows clients to modify specific fields without sending the entire resource, reducing bandwidth and avoiding conflicts. Example: PATCH /users/123 with {"email": "new@example.com"}.
pass.reasoning: Clear explanation with glossary reference, rationale, and example.

partial.excerpt: Implement proper HATEOAS with HAL+JSON hypermedia controls for level 3 REST compliance.
partial.reasoning: Technically correct but assumes significant prior knowledge of REST maturity models.

fail.excerpt: You obviously need to use idempotent methods correctly. Any competent developer knows this.
fail.reasoning: Condescending tone and assumes knowledge without explaining.
